newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist starts journey home after record.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist starts journey home after record.

text.p: Adventurer Steve Fossett set out on Tuesday on his long return journey to the United States, saying someone would fly around the world in a balloon within three years but declining to say if he would try himself.

After flying halfway around the world, Fossett managed to have his tattered, $300,000 balloon pulled down from a tree in a remote Indian field before leaving the landing site on a 13,000-km (8,000-mile) trip home.
It took the 52-year-old commodity broker six days, two hours and 49 minutes to reach India after taking off from the U.S. heartland.
It took another day and a half to pull down the balloon and pack the deflated bladder, propane cylinders and yellow fibreglass cabin onto two wagons pulled by tractors.
Villagers scampered up the "mahua" tree and rescue workers climbed fire brigade ladders to free the "Solo Spirit" from the branches.

Later, the equipment was to be loaded into a police truck that would move it some 150 km (95 miles) to the holy Hindu city of Varanasi, from where Fossett said it would be flown back to the United States.

"I'm feeling great," a relaxed Fossett told Reuters before he left at sunset on Tuesday in a car, escorted by two police vehicles, from his landing site in Nonkhar village for Varanasi, where he was set to spend the night.
Nonkhar is some 550 km (330 miles) southeast of the Indian capital and more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from St Louis, Missouri, where he began his ascent on January 13.

Fossett said he would eventually fly to New Delhi from Varanasi before returning to the United States, but his schedule depended on how long it would take to prepare the balloon and equipment in Varanasi for air shipment.

Fossett said he was happy to have broken two ballooning records -- the greatest distance and longest time in the air -- before running short of fuel, and he called his aborted mission a success. "It's a grand success," he said.
"There are a number of competing teams to try and make it around the world and I think one of them will succeed within three years," Fossett said.

"My team has the most experience with this kind of flight. We certainly have a good chance of being the first person to do it," he earlier told Reuters outside a government guest house in nearby Sultanpur where he spent the night.
But he declined to say whether he himself would make a fresh bid. "I haven't made up my mind as yet, but perhaps I would," he said.
Fossett said villagers who watched in disbelief as his balloon descended onto the Ganges River plain on Monday were of great help.

"When I landed here, people looked a little apprehensive because I could not communicate with anyone as no one spoke English," he said. "But finally some more people came, to whom I could explain who I am and why I am here."
Shiv Kumar Mishra, 15, said many villagers were stunned by the appearance of the balloon.
"We ran when we saw this thing hovering around this place," Mishra said. "Many of us thought that it was a temple sent from the heavens by the gods."
